PESHAWAR: The Peshawar High Court on Wednesday rejected a petition filed by Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi challenging proceedings initiated against him by the Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) for allegedly violating the election code of conduct during by-elections in Haripur in November 2025.

A bench comprising Justice Syed Arshad Ali and Justice Muhammad Faheem Wali pronounced a short order dismissing the petition without touching the question of the ECP's jurisdiction in light of an earlier court order.

The detailed judgement will be issued later.

With the dismissal of the petition, a stay order earlier granted in favour of Mr Afridi also stands vacated.

Following the preliminary hearing of the petition earlier this year, the court had ordered, "In the meanwhile, the respondent-ECP may proceed with the matter; however, it shall not pass any final order adverse to the petitioner (Sohail Afridi) till further orders."

The development assumes significance amid growing tensions between KP and federal governments over the ongoing protest march.

A panel of lawyers appeared for the petitioner, including Adnan Ali, Bashir Khan Wazir, Barrister Sarwar Muzaffar Shah and Inam Yousafzai. The ECP was represented by Additional Director General (Law) Khurram Shehzad and Additional Director (Law) Samran Jehangir, while Barrister Sajeel Sheharyar Swati appeared for the complainant against Mr Afridi before the ECP.

In November last year, the chief minister and by-election candidate Shehrnaz Omar Ayub, backed by PTI, had challenged notices issued to them by the ECP for allegedly violating the election code of conduct.

Mr Afridi had challenged a notice issued to him by the ECP on Nov 20, accusing him of delivering a provocative speech against government functionaries in connection with the by-election in NA-18 Haripur.

The ECP contended that the CM's speech was contrary to the code of conduct issued by the commission for the by-election.

Mr Afridi had asked the high court to set aside the impugned notice. However, on Nov 26, the court dismissed both petitions, observing that no adverse order had so far been passed against the petitioners.

The bench had observed that it expected the ECP, in the first instance, to determine its jurisdiction in the matter before proceeding further with the inquiry.

Mr Afridi again approached the court earlier this year, contending that the ECP had been proceeding against him without first deciding the question of its jurisdiction, contrary to the Elections Act, 2017.

ECP counsel Khurram Shehzad argued that the petition was not maintainable and was liable to be dismissed as no order had so far been passed against the petitioner.

He submitted that the proceedings pending before the commission were independent in nature and separate from those pending before the district monitoring officer (DMO).

He argued that the ECP had two types of jurisdiction — one concerning civil wrongs and the other concerning cases of a criminal nature.

Under Section 15 of the Elections Act, 2017, he said, the ECP could take cognisance of matters relating to implementation of the code of conduct on its own motion as well as on a complaint filed by an aggrieved person.

He contended that an almost identical petition had been dismissed by the court in November last year.

Mr Afridi's counsel, Adnan Ali, stated that the ECP had issued the controversial notice to the chief minister on Nov 20, 2025.

"The allegation pertained to remarks made against election staff and influencing the election," he said.

"The speech delivered by the chief minister was outside the jurisdiction of NA-18 Haripur, where the by-election was held on Nov 23, 2025," the counsel argued.

He said that once the DMO had issued a notice to Mr Afridi under Section 234 of the Elections Act, the ECP lacked jurisdiction to issue another notice to him under Section 15 of the Act.

He argued that the ECP had clubbed a private complaint filed by a rival candidate with its suo motu proceedings. He contended that the ECP was exercising the powers of the DMO. "Here, both the ECP and the DMO issued notices, and the DMO also submitted a report to the former," he argued.

"Let the Election Commission hear you; present whatever your response is before them," Justice Arshad Ali remarked.

The bench observed, "This is merely an inquiry by the Election Commission, not a formal action. There is no legal bar preventing the Election Commission from conducting an inquiry."

However, Mr Afridi's lawyers maintained that the ECP had initiated a process under which the petitioner could face disqualification.

PESHAWAR: The Peshawar High Court on Wednesday rejected a petition filed by Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi challenging proceedings initiated against him by the Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) for allegedly violating the election code of conduct during by-elections in Haripur in November 2025.

A bench comprising Justice Syed Arshad Ali and Justice Muhammad Faheem Wali pronounced a short order dismissing the petition without touching the question of the ECP's jurisdiction in light of an earlier court order.

The detailed judgement will be issued later.

With the dismissal of the petition, a stay order earlier granted in favour of Mr Afridi also stands vacated.

Following the preliminary hearing of the petition earlier this year, the court had ordered, "In the meanwhile, the respondent-ECP may proceed with the matter; however, it shall not pass any final order adverse to the petitioner (Sohail Afridi) till further orders."

The development assumes significance amid growing tensions between KP and federal governments over the ongoing protest march.

A panel of lawyers appeared for the petitioner, including Adnan Ali, Bashir Khan Wazir, Barrister Sarwar Muzaffar Shah and Inam Yousafzai. The ECP was represented by Additional Director General (Law) Khurram Shehzad and Additional Director (Law) Samran Jehangir, while Barrister Sajeel Sheharyar Swati appeared for the complainant against Mr Afridi before the ECP.

In November last year, the chief minister and by-election candidate Shehrnaz Omar Ayub, backed by PTI, had challenged notices issued to them by the ECP for allegedly violating the election code of conduct.

Mr Afridi had challenged a notice issued to him by the ECP on Nov 20, accusing him of delivering a provocative speech against government functionaries in connection with the by-election in NA-18 Haripur.

The ECP contended that the CM's speech was contrary to the code of conduct issued by the commission for the by-election.

Mr Afridi had asked the high court to set aside the impugned notice. However, on Nov 26, the court dismissed both petitions, observing that no adverse order had so far been passed against the petitioners.

The bench had observed that it expected the ECP, in the first instance, to determine its jurisdiction in the matter before proceeding further with the inquiry.

Mr Afridi again approached the court earlier this year, contending that the ECP had been proceeding against him without first deciding the question of its jurisdiction, contrary to the Elections Act, 2017.

ECP counsel Khurram Shehzad argued that the petition was not maintainable and was liable to be dismissed as no order had so far been passed against the petitioner.

He submitted that the proceedings pending before the commission were independent in nature and separate from those pending before the district monitoring officer (DMO).

He argued that the ECP had two types of jurisdiction — one concerning civil wrongs and the other concerning cases of a criminal nature.

Under Section 15 of the Elections Act, 2017, he said, the ECP could take cognisance of matters relating to implementation of the code of conduct on its own motion as well as on a complaint filed by an aggrieved person.

He contended that an almost identical petition had been dismissed by the court in November last year.

Mr Afridi's counsel, Adnan Ali, stated that the ECP had issued the controversial notice to the chief minister on Nov 20, 2025.

"The allegation pertained to remarks made against election staff and influencing the election," he said.

"The speech delivered by the chief minister was outside the jurisdiction of NA-18 Haripur, where the by-election was held on Nov 23, 2025," the counsel argued.

He said that once the DMO had issued a notice to Mr Afridi under Section 234 of the Elections Act, the ECP lacked jurisdiction to issue another notice to him under Section 15 of the Act.

He argued that the ECP had clubbed a private complaint filed by a rival candidate with its suo motu proceedings. He contended that the ECP was exercising the powers of the DMO. "Here, both the ECP and the DMO issued notices, and the DMO also submitted a report to the former," he argued.

"Let the Election Commission hear you; present whatever your response is before them," Justice Arshad Ali remarked.

The bench observed, "This is merely an inquiry by the Election Commission, not a formal action. There is no legal bar preventing the Election Commission from conducting an inquiry."

However, Mr Afridi's lawyers maintained that the ECP had initiated a process under which the petitioner could face disqualification.

PARIS: The French government said on Wednesday it was pausing the use of stun grenades in its policing of student protests, after a 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a clash with riot police, fuelling protesters' accusations of police brutality.

Protests showed no sign of easing, with more than 500 schools closed a day after demonstrations swept across the country, and unions representing high-school students, teachers and other workers planning more marches for Thursday.

The wave of protests has been going on for more than two weeks and has exposed widespread public anger six months ahead of an election to replace President Emmanuel Macron. Speaking to the nation on Wednesday evening, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the government would review the demands made by students and present proposals at the end of October on issues ranging from renovating buildings to make more teachers available, but gave no details.

"In the past, too many promises were not kept, quite simply because they were untenable," Lecornu said. "What I want are concrete, quick and fully funded answers." The lack of an immediate government response, which was decried by student leaders after talks at the education ministry earlier on Wednesday, appeared unlikely to quell the protests.

At Lycee Lamartine, a high school in central Paris, protesters sang the Marseillaise, chanted slogans and performed Mexican waves as they blockaded the entrance to the school.

"We saw there were lots of crumbling walls, a shortage of teachers in public schools, absent teachers," said Gabriel Fillieule, who used to attend a public school but now goes to a private one. He and others said they were protesting to demand better learning conditions for all.

ATHENS: Western civilisation is at a crossroads as it faces multiple threats, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in Athens on Wednesday, calling for a rebuilding of alliances and for Europe to "awaken from its long slumber".

"We are at an inflection point... not only in the history of my nation but an inflection point in the whole of our civilisation," Rubio said in a speech beneath the Acropolis. Mr Rubio insisted on the US right to flex its "national power" in a fiery speech. "Either we choose to act now, or lose the choice to act at all," the top US diplomat said.

The western world must embrace "national power" and technological innovation or risk sliding into decline, he said. His speech, packed with praise for ancient heroes such as Alexander the Great, follows an address in February where he argued that Europe was threatened by mass immigration and called for it to defend Christian civilisation.

The United States under President Donald Trump has made its choice, according to Rubio. "We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power: to take back control of our critical supply chains, to reindustrialise our economy, to rebuild our defence, to fight for dominance of the technologies and industries of the future," he said.

"There is new competition between great powers again. There is vulnerability, aggression, terrorism, a whole universe of new threats and attacks again," Rubio said. "We must rebuild our institutions and our alliances to face these threats together," he said.

Rubio said that in Europe he saw encouraging signs of what Washington hoped "will be the beginning of a generational shift, skyrocketing defence spending, a flurry of new partnerships and programmes, expanded manufacturing and production." "We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was lit here millennia ago," he said.

His speech, which was packed with praise for the ancient Greeks, followed an address in February when he argued that Europe was threatened by mass immigration and called for it to defend Christian civilisation. Rubio, who arrived from Iceland as part of a European tour, underlined the "critical" US alliance with Greece. He flagged the energy sector, and announced a joint agreement on information-sharing on drug trafficking and terrorism.

"As you see a world that faces... destabilising events, you recognise how important this alliance with Greece is to the United States," he said, referencing conflict in the Middle East and the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

In the Middle East, he argued that Iran had "lost complete control" of the strategic Strait of Hormuz, seeking to offer reassurance at a time when the United States is struggling to find a way out of the war just weeks before key US legislative elections. Rubio took part in a "strategic dialogue" with Greece on regional and energy security amid high tensions triggered by the wars in Iran and Ukraine. He is to meet conservative Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis, before departing for Lisbon.

The western world must embrace "national power" and technological innovation or risk sliding into decline, he said. His speech, packed with praise for ancient heroes such as Alexander the Great, follows an address in February where he argued that Europe was threatened by mass immigration and called for it to defend Christian civilisation.

The United States under President Donald Trump has made its choice, according to Rubio. "We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power: to take back control of our critical supply chains, to reindustrialise our economy, to rebuild our defence, to fight for dominance of the technologies and industries of the future," he said.

"There is new competition between great powers again. There is vulnerability, aggression, terrorism, a whole universe of new threats and attacks again," Rubio said. "We must rebuild our institutions and our alliances to face these threats together," he said.

Rubio said that in Europe he saw encouraging signs of what Washington hoped "will be the beginning of a generational shift, skyrocketing defence spending, a flurry of new partnerships and programmes, expanded manufacturing and production." "We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was lit here millennia ago," he said.

His speech, which was packed with praise for the ancient Greeks, followed an address in February when he argued that Europe was threatened by mass immigration and called for it to defend Christian civilisation. Rubio, who arrived from Iceland as part of a European tour, underlined the "critical" US alliance with Greece. He flagged the energy sector, and announced a joint agreement on information-sharing on drug trafficking and terrorism.

"As you see a world that faces... destabilising events, you recognise how important this alliance with Greece is to the United States," he said, referencing conflict in the Middle East and the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

Rubio took part in a "strategic dialogue" with Greece on regional and energy security amid high tensions triggered by the wars in Iran and Ukraine. He is to meet conservative Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis, before departing for Lisbon.

ISLAMABAD: The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has extended electronic production monitoring to the leather, paper and paperboard sectors, authorising four private vendors to install and operate camera-based monitoring systems across industrial sectors.

The move is part of the FBR's efforts to strengthen sales tax monitoring and curb tax evasion by obtaining production data directly from manufacturing units rather than relying solely on figures declared by registered manufacturers. The monitoring system is already operating in several industries.

The expansion brought additional manufacturing sectors into a system through which the tax authority can directly observe production activity and maintain records of factory operations, reducing its dependence on production figures declared by registered manufacturers.

The FBR issued SRO 1751 of 2026 on Wednesday to notify that production by registered manufacturers of leather and paper and paperboard would be electronically monitored under Chapter XIV BA of the Sales Tax Rules 2006.

In a separate authorisation, the FBR approved four vendors to supply, install, operate and maintain production-monitoring equipment across five sectors — packaged tea, household electronics, paper and paperboard, edible oil and ghee, and leather.

Obsidian Technologies will monitor textile spinning, while Tollink Pakistan covers aerated beverages and bottled water. ISSM Labelling Solutions monitors textile spinning, tiles, packaged milk, packaged juices and bottled water, while Authentik covers aerated beverages, packaged milk, packaged juices and bottled water.

Under the new arrangement, IP cameras and Network Video Recorders (NVRs) will be installed at production lines. The cameras will continuously capture production activity in real time, while the NVRs will retain recordings for at least two months.

The vendors will be responsible for procuring, installing, operating, maintaining and repairing the equipment. The authorisation is limited to IP cameras and NVRs, barring vendors from supplying or charging manufacturers for any other equipment or software.

All footage and recordings will remain the property of the FBR and will be treated as confidential, with sharing prohibited except as directed by the Board.

The FBR has introduced an online facility allowing steel melters and re-rollers to declare electricity consumption to calculate their sales tax liability when power distribution companies fail to report supplies or submit returns late.

Annex K of the sales tax return is mandatory for steel melters, re-rollers, and composite units to calculate sales tax liability under the Thirteenth Schedule of the Sales Tax Act 1990. The automated system normally obtains electricity consumption data after distribution companies file Annex C of their returns.

However, the FBR said taxpayers were facing difficulties when distribution companies either did not declare electricity supplied to them or filed their returns late, preventing the required consumption data from being automatically reflected in Annex K.

ISLAMABAD: The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has extended electronic production monitoring to the leather, paper and paperboard sectors, authorising four private vendors to install and operate camera-based monitoring systems across industrial sectors.

The move is part of the FBR's efforts to strengthen sales tax monitoring and curb tax evasion by obtaining production data directly from manufacturing units rather than relying solely on figures declared by registered manufacturers. The monitoring system is already operating in several industries.

The expansion brought additional manufacturing sectors into a system through which the tax authority can directly observe production activity and maintain records of factory operations, reducing its dependence on production figures declared by registered manufacturers.

The FBR issued SRO 1751 of 2026 on Wednesday to notify that production by registered manufacturers of leather and paper and paperboard would be electronically monitored under Chapter XIV BA of the Sales Tax Rules 2006.

In a separate authorisation, the FBR approved four vendors to supply, install, operate and maintain production-monitoring equipment across five sectors — packaged tea, household electronics, paper and paperboard, edible oil and ghee, and leather.

Obsidian Technologies will monitor textile spinning, while Tollink Pakistan covers aerated beverages and bottled water. ISSM Labelling Solutions monitors textile spinning, tiles, packaged milk, packaged juices and bottled water, while Authentik covers aerated beverages, packaged milk, packaged juices and bottled water.

Under the new arrangement, IP cameras and Network Video Recorders (NVRs) will be installed at production lines. The cameras will continuously capture production activity in real time, while the NVRs will retain recordings for at least two months.

The vendors will be responsible for procuring, installing, operating, maintaining and repairing the equipment. The authorisation is limited to IP cameras and NVRs, barring vendors from supplying or charging manufacturers for any other equipment or software.

All footage and recordings will remain the property of the FBR and will be treated as confidential, with sharing prohibited except as directed by the Board.

The FBR has introduced an online facility allowing steel melters and re-rollers to declare electricity consumption to calculate their sales tax liability when power distribution companies fail to report supplies or submit returns late.

Annex K of the sales tax return is mandatory for steel melters, re-rollers, and composite units to calculate sales tax liability under the Thirteenth Schedule of the Sales Tax Act 1990. The automated system normally obtains electricity consumption data after distribution companies file Annex C of their returns.

However, the FBR said taxpayers were facing difficulties when distribution companies either did not declare electricity supplied to them or filed their returns late, preventing the required consumption data from being automatically reflected in Annex K.

Informed sources told Dawn that the reopening of independent power producers' (IPPs) contracts and recent legal developments involving K-Electric had heightened risk perception among prospective bidders — both local and foreign — currently undertaking due diligence of the first batch of Discos.

Interestingly, the prime minister's adviser on privatisation, Muhammad Ali — who was involved in renegotiations with IPPs that led to revised contracts during the PTI and PML-N tenures — now faces questions from prospective investors over regulatory and contractual guarantees.

Against this backdrop, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb on Wednesday presided over a meeting of the Steering Committee on Power Sector Regulatory Regime and Reform Options to advance reforms to strengthen the power sector's regulatory framework and promote efficiency, investment, competition and greater private-sector participation.

The finance minister noted that the evolving power sector landscape required a regulatory framework capable of responding to technological developments while supporting efficiency, investment, consumer interests and greater private-sector participation, an official statement said.

The meeting coincided with a stay order on Wednesday from the Sindh High Court against recent decision of the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra) and its appellant tribunal regarding K-Electric's Multi-Year Tariff (MYT) that effectively curtailed federal government's subsidy to KE worth around Rs200 billion. Aggrieved by the appellant tribunal and Nepra decision, KE had challenged it in SHC which suspended those notifications and orders and issued notices to the respondents for next date of hearing on Oct 15.

ISLAMABAD: To attract bidders for the successful privatisation of distribution companies (Discos) and allay concerns about contract sanctity, the government is expediting measures to improve regulatory predictability and considering political risk guarantees from multilateral agencies.

Informed sources told Dawn that the reopening of independent power producers' (IPPs) contracts and recent legal developments involving K-Electric had heightened risk perception among prospective bidders — both local and foreign — currently undertaking due diligence of the first batch of Discos.

They have stressed the need for binding legal guarantees and clear financial risk allocation to prevent post-privatisation contractual disputes, and demanded longer licence tenures than the existing 20-year term for Discos.

Interestingly, the prime minister's adviser on privatisation, Muhammad Ali — who was involved in renegotiations with IPPs that led to revised contracts during the PTI and PML-N tenures — now faces questions from prospective investors over regulatory and contractual guarantees.

Against this backdrop, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb on Wednesday presided over a meeting of the Steering Committee on Power Sector Regulatory Regime and Reform Options to advance reforms to strengthen the power sector's regulatory framework and promote efficiency, investment, competition and greater private-sector participation.

The finance minister noted that the evolving power sector landscape required a regulatory framework capable of responding to technological developments while supporting efficiency, investment, consumer interests and greater private-sector participation, an official statement said.

The meeting coincided with a stay order on Wednesday from the Sindh High Court against recent decision of the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra) and its appellant tribunal regarding K-Electric's Multi-Year Tariff (MYT) that effectively curtailed federal government's subsidy to KE worth around Rs200 billion. Aggrieved by the appellant tribunal and Nepra decision, KE had challenged it in SHC which suspended those notifications and orders and issued notices to the respondents for next date of hearing on Oct 15.

Presiding over a meeting on Pakistan Railways on Wednesday, the prime minister appreciated the efforts of teams from the National Accountability Bureau (NAB) and the Ministry of Railways, led by the NAB chairman, to identify and recover encroached railway land, the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) said.

"Modernising ML-1 is of key importance for the development of Pakistan Railways, improving passenger services and increasing freight transport," he was quoted as saying.

The prime minister directed that ML-1 be developed on a commercial basis by utilising identified railway land worth billions of rupees.

"The real commercial potential of railway properties needs to be harnessed," he said, calling for the effective use of valuable railway land for commercial purposes to contribute to the national economy and the development of Pakistan Railways.

He said corporate-style reforms to strengthen the railways and make it economically self-sufficient were among the government's priorities. He added that the railway minister was working to make the organisation profitable and improve its operations.

Mr Shehbaz, during the meeting, approved securing bank financing through commercial projects on railway land and utilising the funds for the project.

He directed authorities to present a comprehensive plan within two weeks based on the actual commercial potential of railway land.

The meeting was informed that the 1,726-kilometre ML-1 upgrade had been divided into four major sections: Karachi-Rohri, Rohri-Multan, Multan-Lahore and Lahore-Peshawar.

International financing was being used for the Karachi-Rohri section, while plans were being prepared to finance the remaining sections through domestic resources, the meeting was told.

Officials briefed the meeting on various stages of the ML-1 project, progress on the Karachi-Rohri section and railway-owned land, as per the PMO.

Civil work on the first phase of the ML-1 is likely to begin in January 2027. It covers the 480km Karachi-Rohri/Sukkur section, where new up and down tracks will be laid along with fencing on both sides to prevent unauthorised access by people, animals and vehicles.

Presiding over a meeting on Pakistan Railways on Wednesday, the prime minister appreciated the efforts of teams from the National Accountability Bureau (NAB) and the Ministry of Railways, led by the NAB chairman, to identify and recover encroached railway land, the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) said.

"Modernising ML-1 is of key importance for the development of Pakistan Railways, improving passenger services and increasing freight transport," he was quoted as saying.

The prime minister directed that ML-1 be developed on a commercial basis by utilising identified railway land worth billions of rupees.

"The real commercial potential of railway properties needs to be harnessed," he said, calling for the effective use of valuable railway land for commercial purposes to contribute to the national economy and the development of Pakistan Railways.

He said corporate-style reforms to strengthen the railways and make it economically self-sufficient were among the government's priorities. He added that the railway minister was working to make the organisation profitable and improve its operations.

Mr Shehbaz, during the meeting, approved securing bank financing through commercial projects on railway land and utilising the funds for the project.

He directed authorities to present a comprehensive plan within two weeks based on the actual commercial potential of railway land.

The meeting was informed that the 1,726-kilometre ML-1 upgrade had been divided into four major sections: Karachi-Rohri, Rohri-Multan, Multan-Lahore and Lahore-Peshawar.

International financing was being used for the Karachi-Rohri section, while plans were being prepared to finance the remaining sections through domestic resources, the meeting was told.

Officials briefed the meeting on various stages of the ML-1 project, progress on the Karachi-Rohri section and railway-owned land, as per the PMO.

Civil work on the first phase of the ML-1 is likely to begin in January 2027. It covers the 480km Karachi-Rohri/Sukkur section, where new up and down tracks will be laid along with fencing on both sides to prevent unauthorised access by people, animals and vehicles.

PARIS: Mass protests over decrepit conditions at France's high schools descended into sporadic violence on Tuesday, leading to nearly 500 arrests and prompting President Emmanuel Macron to call an emergency meeting. The protests started in late September with students blocking entrances to hundreds of high schools for 15- to 17-year-olds over complaints of dilapidated facilities and teacher shortages.

US President Donald Trump weighed in on Tuesday to blame the unrest in France on "mass migration" and Islam, as he pushed his global right-wing narrative ahead of tough midterm elections at home. In France, parents, teachers and union workers joined the high school students' movement in the capital Paris and other cities.

The interior ministry said 256,000 people protested nationwide, while union organisers put the figure at 450,000. Macron was expected to meet top officials on Tuesday, including Interior Minister Laurent Nunez and Education Minister Edouard Geffray, in response to the unrest, a government source said. At least 488 people were arrested and 43 members of the security forces were wounded on Tuesday, the interior ministry announced. Rights groups, unions and the students have accused authorities of using disproportionate force. A teenager lost a hand on Monday after police fired a stun grenade.

A 14-year-old student in northwest Paris was hit in the face with a tear gas grenade at such close range that he lost several teeth. A policeman was charged Tuesday over that incident.

The decision to put former US Army Major Nidal Hasan to death by army firing squad was approved by the president at the recommendation of Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said on X.

Parnell noted that Hasan killed 12 unarmed active-duty soldiers and a retired serviceman, and wounded 32 others. The secretary of the army will set the time and place of the execution, Parnell said.

A military jury sentenced Hasan to death in August 2013, after finding him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder for opening fire with a laser-sighted handgun in a medical facility at the sprawling central Texas military base.

The shooting came weeks before Hasan, now 56, was scheduled to be deployed to Afghanistan. He was left partially paralysed and confined to a wheelchair.

In a statement responding to Trump's decision, the group Death Penalty Action, which opposes capital punishment, said: "There is nothing Donald Trump loves more than the power to kill." Military executions are rare, and under the Uniform Code of Military Justice a death sentence imposed by court-martial may not be carried out "until approved by the president."

A fifth source, also speaking on condition of anonymity, said Britain was still hopeful that an agreement could be reached to prevent the consulate from closing. If it did close, the source added, London was not expected to take any action until after Israel's Oct 27 election, if at all.

After Britain announced the sanctions, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar accused London of interfering in this month's election. A spokesperson for Saar said on Monday the consulate would close on Thursday.

The British sanctions announcement, and Israel's response, mark a new low in the relationship between the once steadfast allies. Britain has repeatedly criticised Israel over its actions in the war in Gaza and over Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians. Israel's government has accused Britain's governing Labour Party of being hostile towards Israel.

The British consulate, in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood of East Jerusalem, handles the country's relations with Palestinians in the city as well as in the West Bank and Gaza. It also provides consular services to Palestinians. The consulate has been in Jerusalem for almost 200 years, long before the State of Israel was established in 1948.

Britain's top national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, had quietly visited Israel last week in an attempt to keep the consulate open but failed to reach an agreement. Two other sources said that Britain has asked European countries to raise the issue with Israel in hope of convincing the government to reverse its decision.

A search operation was launched 70 nautical miles east of the coastal town of Byala, authorities said. Both vessels are Turkish-owned, according to the Equasis merchant shipping database.

input:
MANCHHAR lake is filling up, but for families who live around it, that has brought little relief. Pakistan's largest freshwater lake receives polluted water from the Main Nara Valley Drain at 2,000 cusecs a day. More Indus water has lowered salinity from about 6,000 to 4,000 TDS, but the lake remains contaminated. For local communities, this means fewer fish to catch, less income to bring home and drinking water that cannot be relied on. Many families that once depended on fishing and other lake-based work are struggling to survive, while dozens of reverse-osmosis plants in settlements are not working. A lake that should sustain the people around it is instead becoming a source of hardship. A higher water level may make Manchhar look healthier from a distance. Up close, the people living beside it know otherwise.

None of this is unknown. Experts have long called for polluted drainage to be diverted away from Manchhar and for the RBOD-II drainage project to be completed so harmful flows can be carried towards the sea. Yet the work has dragged on while the lake has deteriorated and livelihoods have disappeared. The first duty of the state is clear: restore safe drinking-water supplies, repair broken RO plants and provide health support to affected communities. But relief alone is not enough. Sindh and federal authorities need a firm timetable for stopping contaminated inflows and completing the drainage works, with public reporting on water quality and progress. Fisherfolk who have lost their earnings will need support while the lake recovers. Every delay leaves more families with less to live on and fewer reasons to believe official promises. Manchhar can still be restored, but not by allowing pollution to continue and hoping fresh water will hide the damage. The source must be stopped. The people around the lake have already waited far too long.

KARACHI: After a sluggish overnight start stemming from regional and political uncertainty, the Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) on Tuesday saw strong buying interest at attractive valuations, helping the benchmark KSE-100 index recover from recent lows to above the 168,000 level, apparently supported by expectations of a positive conclusion to the ongoing review talks with the visiting International Monetary Fund staff mission.

Media reports suggest negotiations with the IMF are set to conclude on a positive note later this week, paving the way for the disbursement of about $1.2 billion under two programmes — the $7bn Extended Fund Facility (EFF) and the $1.4bn Res­il­ience and Sustainability Facility (RSF).

Topline Securities Ltd said the KSE-100 index rebounded sharply, gaining 2,593 points, or 1.56 per cent, to close at 168,460. The index traded between 165,652 and 168,626 during the session.

Buying interest returned across major sectors, including banks, oil and gas exploration, cem­ent, automobiles, OMCs, refineries, and power. Heavyweights such as United Bank, Habib Bank, Oil and Gas Development Company, Pakistan Petroleum, Pakistan Oilfield, and Hub Power supported the recovery.

ISLAMABAD: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Tuesday directed the relevant authorities to prepare a comprehensive plan for gas load management and take all necessary measures to ensure uninterrupted gas imports during the winter season, given the regional situation.

The premier issued these instructions while chairing a meeting, said the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) in a statement.

"The prime minister directed officials to develop a comprehensive gas load management plan, take necessary measures in advance, launch a public awareness campaign on its implementation, and ensure uninterrupted gas imports in light of the current regional situation," the PMO said.

The participants were informed that domestic consumers would be given priority for the supply of locally produced gas while RLNG would be prioritised for power generation and industries, it said.

The meeting took place as the authorities struggle to finalise the liquefied natural gas (LNG) import plan for the upcoming three winter months — December to February — amid a challenging supply situation stemming from the US-Iran conflict.

Renewed hostilities in the Middle East have resulted in disruption of major oil and gas supply routes — the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab — and caused fuel prices to rise.

Against this backdrop, gas companies and the Petroleum Division had sought at least 22 import cargoes for the three-month period, but the task force on energy, led by Lt-Gen Zafar Iqbal, has promised no more than 10-12 cargoes of around 100 million cubic feet each on a best-effort basis, using all diplomatic and logistical channels.

The plan will be presented to the prime minister for approval, given the involvement of around $100m per spot cargo and the requirement for consent from the Ministry of Finance and the State Bank of Pakistan.

Later, the premier reviewed affairs of the National Highway Authority (NHA), including ongoing development work on national highways, motorways and expressways.

PM Shehbaz directed that all ongoing NHA projects undergo third-party audit. He also ordered the authorities to formulate a strategy for constructing national highways, motorways and expressways under public-private partnerships.

ISLAMABAD: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Tuesday directed the relevant authorities to prepare a comprehensive plan for gas load management and take all necessary measures to ensure uninterrupted gas imports during the winter season, given the regional situation.

The premier issued these instructions while chairing a meeting, said the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) in a statement.

"The prime minister directed officials to develop a comprehensive gas load management plan, take necessary measures in advance, launch a public awareness campaign on its implementation, and ensure uninterrupted gas imports in light of the current regional situation," the PMO said.

The participants were informed that domestic consumers would be given priority for the supply of locally produced gas while RLNG would be prioritised for power generation and industries, it said.

The meeting took place as the authorities struggle to finalise the liquefied natural gas (LNG) import plan for the upcoming three winter months — December to February — amid a challenging supply situation stemming from the US-Iran conflict.

Renewed hostilities in the Middle East have resulted in disruption of major oil and gas supply routes — the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab — and caused fuel prices to rise.

Against this backdrop, gas companies and the Petroleum Division had sought at least 22 import cargoes for the three-month period, but the task force on energy, led by Lt-Gen Zafar Iqbal, has promised no more than 10-12 cargoes of around 100 million cubic feet each on a best-effort basis, using all diplomatic and logistical channels.

The plan will be presented to the prime minister for approval, given the involvement of around $100m per spot cargo and the requirement for consent from the Ministry of Finance and the State Bank of Pakistan.

Later, the premier reviewed affairs of the National Highway Authority (NHA), including ongoing development work on national highways, motorways and expressways.

PM Shehbaz directed that all ongoing NHA projects undergo third-party audit. He also ordered the authorities to formulate a strategy for constructing national highways, motorways and expressways under public-private partnerships.

The premier issued these instructions while chairing a meeting, said the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) in a statement.

"The prime minister directed officials to develop a comprehensive gas load management plan, take necessary measures in advance, launch a public awareness campaign on its implementation, and ensure uninterrupted gas imports in light of the current regional situation," the PMO said.

The participants were informed that domestic consumers would be given priority for the supply of locally produced gas while RLNG would be prioritised for power generation and industries, it said.

The meeting took place as the authorities struggle to finalise the liquefied natural gas (LNG) import plan for the upcoming three winter months — December to February — amid a challenging supply situation stemming from the US-Iran conflict.

Renewed hostilities in the Middle East have resulted in disruption of major oil and gas supply routes — the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab — and caused fuel prices to rise.

Against this backdrop, gas companies and the Petroleum Division had sought at least 22 import cargoes for the three-month period, but the task force on energy, led by Lt-Gen Zafar Iqbal, has promised no more than 10-12 cargoes of around 100 million cubic feet each on a best-effort basis, using all diplomatic and logistical channels.

The plan will be presented to the prime minister for approval, given the involvement of around $100m per spot cargo and the requirement for consent from the Ministry of Finance and the State Bank of Pakistan.

Later, the premier reviewed affairs of the National Highway Authority (NHA), including ongoing development work on national highways, motorways and expressways.

PM Shehbaz directed that all ongoing NHA projects undergo third-party audit. He also ordered the authorities to formulate a strategy for constructing national highways, motorways and expressways under public-private partnerships.

ISLAMABAD: The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has proposed new rules allowing individuals who file their income tax returns after the due date or extended deadline to be included in the Active Taxpayers' List (ATL) without paying the prescribed surcharge.

The concession, however, will be subject to the condition that the individual undertakes not to purchase, acquire or otherwise obtain ownership or beneficial interest in any property for six months from the date of furnishing the undertaking through the FBR's Inland Revenue Information System (IRIS) portal.

The new rules were issued on Tuesday through SRO1690 of the Income Tax, as draft amendments to the Income Tax Rules 2002. FBR sought feedback from all stakeholders within one week before finalising them.

Under the proposed rule 81B, a new rule (2B) is proposed that provides that an individual who files an income tax return for the latest tax year after the due date or the extended deadline will be eligible for inclusion in the ATL without payment of the surcharge if the taxpayer submits an undertaking through the FBR's IRIS portal.

However, the concession comes with a significant restriction. The taxpayer will have to undertake that he or she will not purchase, acquire or otherwise obtain ownership or beneficial interest in any property for six months.

The six-month restriction will begin from the date appearing on the electronic acknowledgement generated by IRIS after successful submission of the newly prescribed Form ATL-U.

The proposed rules also give the FBR powers to verify whether a taxpayer has complied with the undertaking. The FBR may use information available under the Income Tax Ordinance as well as information received from any authority, agency, registry, financial institution or other lawful source.

If information available with the tax authorities shows that an individual acquired ownership or beneficial interest in a property during the six- month period, the taxpayer will first be provided an electronic opportunity of being heard.

The FBR has also proposed a new undertaking Form ATL-U for taxpayers seeking to avail themselves of the facility. The form will require the individual's name, CNIC or NTN, tax year, date of filing the return, IRIS acknowledgement or reference number and the date on which the undertaking is furnished. Russian presidential envoy for Afghanistan Zamir Kabulov said Moscow regretted that the participants could not agree on the final document.

"When drafting the final joint statement, we encountered one problem, that problem was that our Afghan and Pakistani colleagues didn't see eye to eye," he said.

The Moscow meeting brought together special envoys and senior officials from Afghanistan, China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, with Belarus and Egypt attending as guests. The format dates back to 2016 -17 and has emerged as one of the main regional diplomatic tracks on Afghanistan.

The failure to agree on a joint statement underscored how the worsening Pakistan-Afghanistan dispute is now complicating wider regional efforts to build consensus on Afghanistan.

The tense relations between Islamabad and Kabul were among the key issues discussed at the meeting, with the dispute over terrorism and counterterrorism language ultimately preventing the adoption of the joint document.

Mr Kabulov said the Afghan side objected to references that placed Afghanistan in a terrorist context.

Pakistan's special envoy for Afghanistan, Moha­mmad Sadiq, told the meeting that Islamabad wanted peace and stability in the region and had pursued political and diplomatic engagement with the Taliban leadership to address terrorism emanating from Afghan soil.

"Pakistan desires peace and stability in the region and has remained patiently engaged in political and diplomatic efforts aimed at addressing the menace of terrorism emanating from Afghan soil. However, it is unfortunate that Pakistan's numerous goodwill gestures and highly responsible appr­oach were misconstrued, resulting in increased terrorist attacks from Afghan soil, with the active support and backing of the Taliban Regime," he said.

Afghan Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi, meanwhile, criticised Pakistan's statements and actions towards Afghanistan and Afghans, accusing Islamabad of using military pressure, refugees, students and transit routes as instruments of leverage.

At the same time, he insisted that the problems affecting relations bet­ween the two neighbours could be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy.

Russia offered to help de-escalate the dispute, although Kabulov stressed that resolving bilateral disputes was not the purpose of the Moscow Format.

"Russia is ready to assist in ending this conflict in any possible, permissible way either on its own or in partnership with our other partners provided that both sides make such a request. We are ready to provide the maximum possible assistance," he said.

Informed sources said the two sides were now finalising the Memor­andum of Econ­omic and Fiscal Policies (MEFP) after covering the substantive parameters of the biannual review.

Following the completion of the draft exchanges, the staff mission, led by Ms Iva Petrova, is expected to conclude its visit in the next couple of days, official sources said. There were no new demands from the Fund, except for makeup adjustments to bridge past slippages. The revenue target remains unchanged, with a greater focus on achieving the half-yearly target following robust collection in the first quarter, which exceeded the target.

The development comes as the authorities struggle to finalise the liquefied natural gas (LNG) import plan for the upcoming three winter months — December to February — amid a challenging supply situation stemming from the US-Iran conflict.

ISLAMABAD: As the government reiterated that its doors were open for a dialogue with all political parties, the PTI on Monday said reconciliation with the ruling coalition was not possible without the involvement of jailed party chief Imran Khan.

Addressing a press conference at the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa House in the federal capital, PTI Secretary General Salman Akram Raja said only Imran Khan was able to bridge the gulf "developed between the state and the nation".

"Imran Khan is very important for us and we had every right to seek his opinion, but it was not allowed," Mr Raja said about the recent talks with the government.

The PTI leader said another reason for the failure of the talks was that the government was not willing to pursue a collective strategy against terrorism. "We were being pushed to support the government over every action being taken regarding terrorism in KP," he said, adding that the PTI had demanded that the government respect the recommendations and opinions of a jirga held by the KP Assembly, in which political parties and stakeholders had participated.

"We were told that a unanimous strategy against terrorism would not be developed and it would not be included in the agreement," he said, adding that the government had deliberately complicated the situation.

Federal Parliamentary Secretary for Information and Broadcasting Barrister Danyal Chaudhry said the government firmly believed in reconciliation and made serious efforts to resolve matters through dialogue and negotiation. The PTI sabotaged the negotiation process, he alleged.

Flanked by Prime Minister's Coordinator Ikhtiar Wali Khan, Barrister Danyal said the government engaged the PTI with complete sincerity and made every effort to resolve matters amicably.

"The government is ready to take all political forces along and believes in resolving political differences democratically through dialogue and reconciliation," he said, noting that the PTI lacked clear leadership on negotiations.

On the performance of the PTI government in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, he said serious questions had been raised over the past 15 years regarding governance and law and order in the province. "Corruption flourished in KP while basic facilities and administrative improvements remained elusive," he claimed.

Minister for Kashmir Affairs and Gilgit-Baltistan Amir Muqam, however, said the government's delegation had suggested that both sides "be on the same page" about terrorism.

ISLAMABAD: Members of the Makkah defence pact announced their intention to begin rapid force deployment, aimed at enhancing Saudi Arabia's "readiness, military integration, and the collective capacity to confront and counter threats".

The announcement came as the Riyadh-backed Yemeni government claimed recapturing the key Red Sea port of Mocha, amid its bid to retake control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.

Meanwhile, fighting between the government forces and Houthi militia raged in other parts of the country.

Government forces advanced rapidly along the coast with heavy Saudi air support to seize key positions in the Dhubab area on the narrowest point of the strait, a vital oil route whose seizure by the Iran-backed Houthis last month sent shockwaves through energy markets.

The offensive came against the backdrop of a meeting of the Makkah Defence Alliance in Riyadh, which convened in the Saudi capital to take stock of the Houthi attacks on the kingdom.

Military spokesman Lt Col Majid Abdullah al-Nuzayli said the pro-government forces had "successfully taken control of Bab al-Mandeb". In a series of statements, he said that government forces also took control of Dhubab airport and cut off the road between Dhubab and Mocha. Hundreds of Houthi fighters have been surrounded in the Dhubab area, he said, adding that some Houthi fighters later fled by boat via the sea.

The government offensive was announced on Sunday to recapture territory, with Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi swearing to fight "until the country is liberated from the grip of the terrorist militia".

Saudi Arabia, which arms and trains Yemeni government forces, is backing the military campaign with air power and has sought logistical help from allies to push back the Houthis, restore free traffic in the Red Sea, and end the group's attacks on its territory. Riyadh said on Monday it had attacked hundreds of targets in Yemen to provide air cover for the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and Yemeni ground forces.

"100 fighter jets participated at dawn today in Operation 'Dawn of Yemen'," Saudi-led coalition spokesman Major Gen Turki al-Maliki wrote on X, using the name for the new offensive announced on Sunday.

The Houthi-run health ministry said two people had been killed and seven wounded in strikes on Sanhan and Sa'wan districts in Sanaa province. The renewed fighting has worsened a humanitarian crisis in Yemen, with the UN migration agency saying on Monday that some 184,000 people had now been displaced since the war resumed.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland that Saudi Arabia has a right to defend itself against attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels, Al Jazeera reported.

"Obviously the Saudis have come under Houthi attack … and they have a right to defend themselves", he said, adding that neither Riyadh nor Yemen's internationally recognised government was "in favour of [Houthi] control in that territory". Mr Rubio also stressed that the US intended to honour the security agreement it had with Saudi Arabia.

While the war has raged on several frontlines in Yemen, the heaviest fighting has been in the southwest, both in the coastal area near the strait and in the hills around Taiz, where the Houthis have been battling to surround government forces. Last week Houthi attacks damaged a culvert on the Taiz-Aden road, making it impassable. MADRID: Spain's Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Monday called a snap election for Nov 29, after parliament rejected housing relief measures proposed by his minority government amid nationwide protests.

The defeat on Friday was just the latest political setback for Sanchez, one of the few left-leaning government leaders still in power in Europe. "To do more, we need to renew and broaden the support of the people," Sanchez said in a televised address, adding that his aim was "to secure a much broader, progressive majority in parliament".

The next general election was scheduled to take place by August 2027. His announcement came after tens of thousands of people marched in Madrid and other cities on Saturday demanding action on housing affordability.

The government's proposed measures, which included automatic renewal of tenancy contracts and restrictions on evicting vulnerable tenants, were voted down by opposition parties in Spain's parliament.

The defeat infuriated the protesters and underscored the difficulties Sanchez's minority coalition government faces in passing legislation. The protests were fuelled by the eviction last month of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the Madrid flat where she had lived for decades.

Hundreds of demonstrators have occupied a tent camp in central Madrid for more than a week, demanding housing reforms. One of them, 19-year-old student Sara Prieto Aparicio, said that she believed that calling the snap election "was the best thing to do". "There is a big mobilisation by citizens and I think this favours elections," she said.

"This wave of indignation is unstoppable and we are not going to stop," Alicia del Rio, a spokesperson for the Madrid Tenants' Union, one of the protest leaders, said while renewing a call for a general strike. Recent opinion polls have generally put the main opposition conservative Popular Party (PP) ahead of the Socialists.

The PP would likely need to partner with the far-right Vox to form a government however. Making housing the central campaign issue "could mobilise left-leaning voters", said Federico Santi, a Europe analyst at political risk consultancy Eurasia Group.

He said an early election could help limit further erosion of support for the Socialists, amid resurgent inflation, legislative deadlock and corruption scandals. Housing has become one of Spain's main political issues as supply lags demand.

MADRID: Spain's Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Monday called a snap election for Nov 29, after parliament rejected housing relief measures proposed by his minority government amid nationwide protests.

The defeat on Friday was just the latest political setback for Sanchez, one of the few left-leaning government leaders still in power in Europe. "To do more, we need to renew and broaden the support of the people," Sanchez said in a televised address, adding that his aim was "to secure a much broader, progressive majority in parliament".

The next general election was scheduled to take place by August 2027. His announcement came after tens of thousands of people marched in Madrid and other cities on Saturday demanding action on housing affordability.

The government's proposed measures, which included automatic renewal of tenancy contracts and restrictions on evicting vulnerable tenants, were voted down by opposition parties in Spain's parliament.

The defeat infuriated the protesters and underscored the difficulties Sanchez's minority coalition government faces in passing legislation. The protests were fuelled by the eviction last month of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the Madrid flat where she had lived for decades.

Hundreds of demonstrators have occupied a tent camp in central Madrid for more than a week, demanding housing reforms. One of them, 19-year-old student Sara Prieto Aparicio, said that she believed that calling the snap election "was the best thing to do". "There is a big mobilisation by citizens and I think this favours elections," she said.

"This wave of indignation is unstoppable and we are not going to stop," Alicia del Rio, a spokesperson for the Madrid Tenants' Union, one of the protest leaders, said while renewing a call for a general strike. Recent opinion polls have generally put the main opposition conservative Popular Party (PP) ahead of the Socialists.

The PP would likely need to partner with the far-right Vox to form a government however. Making housing the central campaign issue "could mobilise left-leaning voters", said Federico Santi, a Europe analyst at political risk consultancy Eurasia Group.

He said an early election could help limit further erosion of support for the Socialists, amid resurgent inflation, legislative deadlock and corruption scandals. Housing has become one of Spain's main political issues as supply lags demand.

NADI: Extreme heat is increasingly linked to problems such as premature births or underweight babies, the UN climate chief warned on Monday as Fiji hosted talks ahead of a major summit.

This week's meetings in the city of Nadi and on the atoll nation of Tuvalu are aimed at drawing the world's attention to life on the frontline of climate change in the Pacific.

They are a precursor to the larger UN-sponsored global climate summit — known as COP31 — to be held in Turkiye next month.

Highlighting the need for urgent action, United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell cited a new survey showing more than two-thirds of health professionals across five continents had seen complications caused by intense heat in the past five years.

"Climate-driven extreme heat during pregnancy is increasingly linked to premature birth, stillbirth, low birth weight, and maternal complications," he said.

The Plan International charity said in a separate report on Monday that climate disasters were also increasing the risk of child marriage and teen pregnancies, in part through their impact on the health and education services on which girls depend.

The South Pacific is among the most vulnerable regions in the world to global warming — from rising sea waters jeopardising homes to increasing temperatures causing coral bleaching. Fiji's climate minister Lynda Tabuya called for commitments from developed nations to a "just transition", with support for "countries in the world that suffer the most".

A UN report released in August found developing countries needed $310 billion-$365 billion to adapt, yet had only $26 billion in adaptation finance available in 2023. "We rely on and we appeal to countries to commit to climate finance," Tabuya said. Australia — the head of this year's climate negotiations and a major coal exporter — faces accusations of hypocrisy. Its sales of the fossil fuel have boomed on the back of demand caused by the Middle East conflict.

Tabuya told journalists there had been "frank discussion" on Monday with Australian counterpart Chris Bowen and Pacific officials. "Yes, we have sentiments expressed from certain countries," she said, when asked if she backed calls from other Pacific leaders for Australia to halt expansion of coal and gas projects.

"But for the Pacific, it's important at this pre-COP that we find common ground. There will be things that we disagree on, but we can agree to disagree," Tabuya said.

Also high on the agenda is a push by Pacific leaders for the world to stick to a target of limiting global warming to 1.5C and give more attention to the impact on oceans.

"Keeping 1.5 alive means hope — hope for Tuvalu, hope for Kiribati, hope for small island atolls around the world," Bowen told journalists.

"We can actually come to this conversation and say, 'as a fossil-fuel exporting nation, we can bring something different to the table'," he said. Sea levels are also rising at a record pace, driven by warming oceans and glacier melt, according to the August UN report.

NADI: Extreme heat is increasingly linked to problems such as premature births or underweight babies, the UN climate chief warned on Monday as Fiji hosted talks ahead of a major summit.

This week's meetings in the city of Nadi and on the atoll nation of Tuvalu are aimed at drawing the world's attention to life on the frontline of climate change in the Pacific.

They are a precursor to the larger UN-sponsored global climate summit — known as COP31 — to be held in Turkiye next month.

Highlighting the need for urgent action, United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell cited a new survey showing more than two-thirds of health professionals across five continents had seen complications caused by intense heat in the past five years.

"Climate-driven extreme heat during pregnancy is increasingly linked to premature birth, stillbirth, low birth weight, and maternal complications," he said.

The Plan International charity said in a separate report on Monday that climate disasters were also increasing the risk of child marriage and teen pregnancies, in part through their impact on the health and education services on which girls depend.

The South Pacific is among the most vulnerable regions in the world to global warming — from rising sea waters jeopardising homes to increasing temperatures causing coral bleaching. Fiji's climate minister Lynda Tabuya called for commitments from developed nations to a "just transition", with support for "countries in the world that suffer the most".

A UN report released in August found developing countries needed $310 billion-$365 billion to adapt, yet had only $26 billion in adaptation finance available in 2023. "We rely on and we appeal to countries to commit to climate finance," Tabuya said. Australia — the head of this year's climate negotiations and a major coal exporter — faces accusations of hypocrisy. Its sales of the fossil fuel have boomed on the back of demand caused by the Middle East conflict.

Tabuya told journalists there had been "frank discussion" on Monday with Australian counterpart Chris Bowen and Pacific officials. "Yes, we have sentiments expressed from certain countries," she said, when asked if she backed calls from other Pacific leaders for Australia to halt expansion of coal and gas projects.

"But for the Pacific, it's important at this pre-COP that we find common ground. There will be things that we disagree on, but we can agree to disagree," Tabuya said.

Also high on the agenda is a push by Pacific leaders for the world to stick to a target of limiting global warming to 1.5C and give more attention to the impact on oceans.

"Keeping 1.5 alive means hope — hope for Tuvalu, hope for Kiribati, hope for small island atolls around the world," Bowen told journalists.

"We can actually come to this conversation and say, 'as a fossil-fuel exporting nation, we can bring something different to the table'," he said. Sea levels are also rising at a record pace, driven by warming oceans and glacier melt, according to the August UN report.

NADI: Extreme heat is increasingly linked to problems such as premature births or underweight babies, the UN climate chief warned on Monday as Fiji hosted talks ahead of a major summit.

This week's meetings in the city of Nadi and on the atoll nation of Tuvalu are aimed at drawing the world's attention to life on the frontline of climate change in the Pacific.

They are a precursor to the larger UN-sponsored global climate summit — known as COP31 — to be held in Turkiye next month.

Highlighting the need for urgent action, United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell cited a new survey showing more than two-thirds of health professionals across five continents had seen complications caused by intense heat in the past five years.

"Climate-driven extreme heat during pregnancy is increasingly linked to premature birth, stillbirth, low birth weight, and maternal complications," he said.

The Plan International charity said in a separate report on Monday that climate disasters were also increasing the risk of child marriage and teen pregnancies, in part through their impact on the health and education services on which girls depend.

The South Pacific is among the most vulnerable regions in the world to global warming — from rising sea waters jeopardising homes to increasing temperatures causing coral bleaching. Fiji's climate minister Lynda Tabuya called for commitments from developed nations to a "just transition", with support for "countries in the world that suffer the most".

A UN report released in August found developing countries needed $310 billion-$365 billion to adapt, yet had only $26 billion in adaptation finance available in 2023. "We rely on and we appeal to countries to commit to climate finance," Tabuya said. Australia — the head of this year's climate negotiations and a major coal exporter — faces accusations of hypocrisy. Its sales of the fossil fuel have boomed on the back of demand caused by the Middle East conflict.

Tabuya told journalists there had been "frank discussion" on Monday with Australian counterpart Chris Bowen and Pacific officials. "Yes, we have sentiments expressed from certain countries," she said, when asked if she backed calls from other Pacific leaders for Australia to halt expansion of coal and gas projects.

"But for the Pacific, it's important at this pre-COP that we find common ground. There will be things that we disagree on, but we can agree to disagree," Tabuya said.

Also high on the agenda is a push by Pacific leaders for the world to stick to a target of limiting global warming to 1.5C and give more attention to the impact on oceans.

"Keeping 1.5 alive means hope — hope for Tuvalu, hope for Kiribati, hope for small island atolls around the world," Bowen told journalists.

"We can actually come to this conversation and say, 'as a fossil-fuel exporting nation, we can bring something different to the table'," he said. Sea levels are also rising at a record pace, driven by warming oceans and glacier melt, according to the August UN report.

THE Kissan Board Pakistan has demanded that agriculture receive at least 10pc of the federal and provincial budgets to lower input costs and address recurring deficits.

The farmers' body also wants support prices of Rs5,000 per 40kg for wheat and Rs700 for sugarcane, citing declining profitability. It has criticised urea shortages, high electricity bills, weak fruit sector returns, and the Pak-Afghan border closure, warning of protests if their demands are not met. Their case for enhanced budgetary allocations deserves consideration. The sector contributes about 22pc of GDP and supports nearly 60pc of the population, but receives only 2-3pc of allocations. However, money alone will not fix matters. Nor should a larger allocation become another excuse for inefficient price subsidies. Pakistan has spent decades trying to support farmers through administered prices, input subsidies and other interventions. This has distorted markets, encouraged inefficient production and benefited better-connected producers more than small farmers.

THE Kissan Board Pakistan has demanded that agriculture receive at least 10pc of the federal and provincial budgets to lower input costs and address recurring deficits.

The farmers' body also wants support prices of Rs5,000 per 40kg for wheat and Rs700 for sugarcane, citing declining profitability. It has criticised urea shortages, high electricity bills, weak fruit sector returns, and the Pak-Afghan border closure, warning of protests if their demands are not met. Their case for enhanced budgetary allocations deserves consideration. The sector contributes about 22pc of GDP and supports nearly 60pc of the population, but receives only 2-3pc of allocations. However, money alone will not fix matters. Nor should a larger allocation become another excuse for inefficient price subsidies. Pakistan has spent decades trying to support farmers through administered prices, input subsidies and other interventions. This has distorted markets, encouraged inefficient production and benefited better-connected producers more than small farmers.

input:
THE new National Cybercrime Investigation Agency chief, Ali Nasir Rizvi, has adopted a "zero-tolerance policy against fake news and anti-state propaganda", according to the agency.

Troublingly, neither 'fake news' nor 'anti-state propaganda' has a clear, legal meaning, and the fact that these terms are now centrepieces in the NCCIA's policy gives rise to concerns about what the state's priorities truly are. The authority's mandate includes protecting citizens from fraud, harassment, blackmail, and financial scams. It recently shut down several fraudulent call centres, showing it can deliver well on those responsibilities. Monitoring and policing opinion are something else altogether.

Further, the fact that the NCCIA has established 'cyber patrolling units' in every region is alarming. Why is the authority engaging in mass public surveillance? What is being monitored, for what purpose, and under what legal authority? Who will be providing oversight, and how will citizens be protected from excessive surveillance? Since the DG has promised merit and transparency, he should satisfy the public in this regard.

It is worth pointing out here that these special units for surveillance sit atop the 2025 Peca amendments, which criminalised spreading 'false' information, amid strong protests from journalists and rights groups. The timing of the announcement also comes amidst a deadlock between the government and the opposition over protests announced by the latter.

In such a charged political environment, the message would seem to be that dissent, not disinformation, is the actual target. It is hoped that the NCCIA will act with restraint and transparency to avoid cementing that perception. The authority must avoid politicising its work.

Misinformation and disinformation do real harm; the answer to them is fast, credible official communication, improved media literacy, and platform accountability, not prosecution and lawfare. The state must build trust with the public if it wishes to defeat what it calls 'fake news' and 'propaganda'.

input:
THE new National Cybercrime Investigation Agency chief, Ali Nasir Rizvi, has adopted a "zero-tolerance policy against fake news and anti-state propaganda", according to the agency.

Troublingly, neither 'fake news' nor 'anti-state propaganda' has a clear, legal meaning, and the fact that these terms are now centrepieces in the NCCIA's policy gives rise to concerns about what the state's priorities truly are. The authority's mandate includes protecting citizens from fraud, harassment, blackmail, and financial scams. It recently shut down several fraudulent call centres, showing it can deliver well on those responsibilities. Monitoring and policing opinion are something else altogether.

Further, the fact that the NCCIA has established 'cyber patrolling units' in every region is alarming. Why is the authority engaging in mass public surveillance? What is being monitored, for what purpose, and under what legal authority? Who will be providing oversight, and how will citizens be protected from excessive surveillance? Since the DG has promised merit and transparency, he should satisfy the public in this regard.

It is worth pointing out here that these special units for surveillance sit atop the 2025 Peca amendments, which criminalised spreading 'false' information, amid strong protests from journalists and rights groups. The timing of the announcement also comes amidst a deadlock between the government and the opposition over protests announced by the latter.

In such a charged political environment, the message would seem to be that dissent, not disinformation, is the actual target. It is hoped that the NCCIA will act with restraint and transparency to avoid cementing that perception. The authority must avoid politicising its work.

Misinformation and disinformation do real harm; the answer to them is fast, credible official communication, improved media literacy, and platform accountability, not prosecution and lawfare. The state must build trust with the public if it wishes to defeat what it calls 'fake news' and 'propaganda'.

ISLAMABAD: Services exports grew by a robust 28.89 per cent year on year in the first two months of 2026-27, largely driven by higher earnings from information technology.

According to official data compiled by the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (PBS), services exports have continued to expand, maintaining uninterrupted growth since the start of FY27, in contrast to mixed trends in goods shipments.

In absolute terms, services exports totalled $1.81 billion in July-August FY27, up from $1.41bn in the corresponding months of last year. In August, services exports rose 28.97pc to $873.01 million, from $676.91m in the corresponding month last year. Telecomm­unications, computer and information services have driven growth since the beginning of the fiscal year.

According to data compiled by the State Bank of Pakistan, exports of telecommunications, computer and information services grew 17.36pc to $811m in 2MFY27 from $691m a year ago.

Exports of other business services surged 38.62pc to $420m in 2MFY27, from $303m in the same period last year. Similarly, exports of transport services increased by 35.87pc to $178m from $131m a year earlier.

However, exports of travel services surged 146.66pc to $222m from $90m in 2MFY26.

At the same time, services imports rose 9.77pc to $2.37bn in 2MFY27, from $2.16bn in the corresponding period last year. In August, services imports rose 2.53pc to $1.15bn, from $1.13bn a year ago.

The board meeting, held on Monday and chaired by Adviser to the Prime Minister on Privatisation Muhammad Ali, was informed that it had received 11 expressions of interest (EoIs) for acquiring 51 per cent to 100pc shareholding, along with management control.

ISLAMABAD: After months of reluctance, the Power Division finally conceded on Monday that the marginal power price had significantly incre­ased 'due to regional war' and the subsidised rates to a select industrial category had burdened other consumer categories.

This came at a public hearing convened by the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra), whose case officers reported that the average power supply cost now stood at Rs32 per unit, compared with Rs22.98 per unit offered to industrial consumers on Dece­mber 10 last year under the Incremental Consum­ption Package.

The Power Division team led by additional secretary Mehfooz Bhatti and Naveed Qaiser, however, warned that its retrospective correction from June 9, as demanded by wider in­dustrial consumers thro­ugh interventions, would need to be legally examined.

The government team generally appeared on the back foot, as Mr Bhatti said the incremental package was announced after almost a year of hard work on industry demand, but nobody could have anticipated a 'war scene' that changed 'economic fundamentals'.

Not only the industrial representatives Rehan Javed, Amir Shaikh, Arif Bilwani and Tanveer Barry but also Nepra members Amina Ahmad, Ghulamullah Shaikh and Maqsood Anwar wondered why the government team had not applied for review of the package on completion of the mandatory six-month period and why it did not work out the latest or average marginal cost.
